about: Adversarial answers for every war_and_peace_book1 question, written 2026-10-03 by three reviewers who checked each against the corpus (chapters I-XIV): three correct answers (terse, cited, hedge-first) and three wrong ones a careless scorer could pass (the right names with the wrong relation, a decline that repeats the terms, a confusable substitute). Scored against the whole corpus, every correct answer must pass and every wrong one fail.

correct: It takes place in July 1805.
Anna Pávlovna Schérer's reception is held in July, 1805; the narrator introduces her as the speaker 'in July, 1805' [[cite:C0:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not give a precise date, but it places the reception in July, 1805.
wrong: It takes place in 1805, some weeks after July, once the Guards had left Petersburg.
The sources do not state the month of the reception, though July and 1805 are both mentioned.
It takes place in August, 1805.

correct: She was maid of honor and favorite of the Empress Márya Fëdorovna.

Anna Pávlovna Schérer is introduced as the well-known hostess who was maid of honor and favorite of the Empress Márya Fëdorovna [[cite:C0:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; the knowledge graph also calls her patroness the Dowager Empress.
The text does not spell out the court post beyond that phrase, but it says she was maid of honor and favorite of the Empress Márya Fëdorovna.
wrong: Márya Fëdorovna was the maid of honor and favorite of Anna Pávlovna Schérer, who received guests at her soirée.
The sources do not say whose favorite she was; Márya Fëdorovna is only mentioned in connection with Baron Funke.
She was maid of honor to the Empress Elizabeth, wife of the Emperor Alexander.

correct: The post of first secretary at Vienna.
Prince Vasíli wanted his son appointed first secretary at Vienna, the post for which the Dowager Empress was being urged to choose Baron Funke [[cite:C1:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not say which of his sons it was, but the post was that of first secretary at Vienna.
wrong: Prince Vasíli wanted to be appointed first secretary at Vienna himself, rather than see Baron Funke get it.
The sources do not say which post he wanted for his son, though Baron Funke is mentioned in connection with a secretary post at Vienna.
He wanted the post of ambassador at Vienna for his son, a higher place than the first secretary post given to Baron Funke.

correct: Forty thousand rubles a year.
Prince Vasíli complains to Anna Pávlovna that Anatole is costing him forty thousand rubles a year and wonders what it will be in five years [[cite:C2:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not give an itemised figure, but Prince Vasíli says Anatole costs him 40,000 rubles a year.
wrong: Prince Vasíli says Anatole costs him forty thousand serfs' worth of income, the size of Count Bezúkhov's estate.
The sources do not state the annual cost, though forty thousand is mentioned in connection with Anatole.
Forty thousand serfs a year.

correct: Caesar's Commentaries.

Lying on the sofa in Prince Andrew's study, Pierre took the first book that came to hand from the shelf, Caesar's Commentaries, and began reading it in the middle [[cite:C0:S3|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not say he chose it deliberately, but the book was Caesar's Commentaries, the first that came to his hand.
wrong: Prince Andrew handed Pierre Caesar's Commentaries when he came into the study.
The sources do not name the book; Caesar is only mentioned in passing in that scene.
He took the Abbé Morio's pamphlet on perpetual peace.

correct: The doll was called Mimi.

Natásha produced a doll from the folds of her frock and, laughing, said "My doll... Mimi..." [[cite:C3:S5|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; Borís later joked that he had known Mimi before her nose was broken.
The text does not state it in a single sentence, but Natásha calls her doll Mimi.
wrong: Mimi was the name of Natásha's younger sister, not the doll.
The context does not name the doll, though Mimi is mentioned in the scene.
The doll was called Sónya, after her cousin.

correct: Dr. Lorrain.
Anna Mikháylovna tells the countess that Count Bezúkhov is so ill he may die at any moment and that Dr. Lorrain has come from Petersburg [[cite:C1:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not describe the doctor further, but the one who came from Petersburg is Dr. Lorrain.
wrong: Dr. Lorrain had been sent by Prince Vasíli from Moscow to attend Pierre.
The sources do not name the doctor attending Count Bezúkhov, beyond a mention of Lorrain.
It was Dr. Métivier, the court physician.

correct: It was near the Horse Guards' barracks.
Pierre drove to Kurágin's that night [[cite:C4:S6|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; the house where Anatole lived stood near the Horse Guards' barracks.
The retrieved text does not describe the house itself, but in the novel it is the large house near the Horse Guards' barracks.
wrong: It was near the Semënov Guards' barracks, where Dólokhov served.
The sources do not say; they only mention the Guards and Kurágin's house in St. Petersburg.
It was on the Moyka Canal, near the Winter Palace.

correct: On the Povarskáya.
The Countess Rostóva's big house, well known to all Moscow, stood on the Povarskáya [[cite:C0:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not call it a street in so many words, but the big house is on the Povarskáya.
wrong: On the Arbat; the Povarskáya is where Count Bezúkhov lives.
The sources do not name the street, though the Povarskáya is mentioned.
On the Tverskáya, near the Povarskáya.

correct: A whole bottle of rum, for fifty imperials.

Dólokhov bet Stevens fifty imperials that he would drink a whole bottle of rum without taking it from his mouth, sitting outside the window and without holding on [[cite:C3:S4|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not call it a single draught in so many words, but the wager was a whole bottle of rum, drunk on the ledge without holding on, for fifty imperials.
wrong: A bottle of rum, for a hundred imperials; fifty was only Stevens's counter-offer.
The sources do not specify the stake, though rum and fifty imperials are mentioned.
A bottle of vodka for fifty imperials.

correct: Into the Moyka Canal.

According to the visitor talking with the count, the young men tied a policeman and the bear back to back and put the bear into the Moyka Canal, where it swam about with the policeman on its back [[cite:C0:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not name a river as such, but the waterway was the Moyka Canal.
wrong: Dólokhov himself was tied to the bear and thrown into the Moyka by the police.
The sources do not state which waterway; the Moyka is mentioned only as a canal in Petersburg.
Into the Neva, the main river of Petersburg.

correct: Cyril Vladímirovich.
Pierre is the illegitimate son of Count Bezúkhov [[cite:C0:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]], whom the text names Count Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov [[cite:C5:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not spell out the patronymic in Pierre's own scene, but his father is Count Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov.
wrong: Pierre's father is Count Ilyá, and Cyril Vladímirovich is Borís's godfather, a different man.
The text does not give his name, though Cyril Vladímirovich is mentioned as Borís's godfather.
Kirill Vladímirovich Bezúkhov.

correct: She had borne twelve children.
The countess, a woman of about forty-five, was worn out with childbearing: she had had twelve [[cite:C0:S4|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not say how many survived, but the countess had borne twelve children.
wrong: She had twelve children, all of whom are present at the name-day party.
The sources do not give a number, although twelve is mentioned in the description of the countess.
She had four children: Véra, Nicholas, Natásha and Pétya.

correct: Colonel Schubert.
The count says that Schubert, the colonel of the Pávlograd Hussars, is dining with them; he has been on leave and is taking Nicholas back with him [[cite:C0:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text gives only his surname, but the colonel is Schubert.
wrong: Schubert is Nicholas's university friend who is joining the Pávlograd Hussars with him; the colonel is not named.
The sources do not name the colonel, though Schubert is mentioned as dining with the count.
Colonel Denísov of the Pávlograd Hussars.

correct: He was nicknamed "the King of Prussia".
Princess Mary's father, the well-known Prince Bolkónski who had to retire from the army under the late Emperor, was nicknamed 'the King of Prussia' [[cite:C3:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not say who coined it, but he was known as 'the King of Prussia.'
wrong: He was called the King of Prussia because he served the King of Prussia after retiring; Prince Vasíli gave him the nickname.
The sources do not give a nickname, although the King of Prussia is mentioned.
He was nicknamed 'the bear'.

correct: La grippe.
Anna Pávlovna said she was suffering from la grippe, then a new word in St. Petersburg used only by the elite [[cite:C1:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not name a medical diagnosis, but she called her illness 'la grippe'.
wrong: Influenza, which the elite then called the grippe in Moscow.
The sources do not name her illness, though the word grippe is mentioned.
A cough - she had had a cough for some days.

correct: The illness of the wealthy old Count Bezúkhov and the misconduct of his illegitimate son Pierre.

The chief topic of the day was Count Bezúkhov's illness and the scandal around his illegitimate son Pierre, who had behaved so improperly at Anna Pávlovna's reception [[cite:C5:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not call it gossip in so many words, but the chief topic among the callers was Count Bezúkhov's illness and his son Pierre's behavior.
wrong: Pierre Bezúkhov's engagement to Prince Vasíli's daughter.
The sources do not record the callers' gossip, though Bezúkhov and Pierre are mentioned elsewhere.
The news that war had been declared against Bonaparte.

correct: Madame de Genlis.
Nicholas had nicknamed Véra "Madame de Genlis", a name considered very stinging [[cite:C1:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not show the shouting in this passage, but the nickname Nicholas gave Véra was Madame de Genlis.
wrong: Véra gave Natásha the nickname Madame de Genlis.
The context does not state the nickname, though Madame de Genlis is mentioned.
They called her 'the countess', after her mother.

correct: The Abbé Morio's.
Pierre told Anna Pávlovna he had heard of the Abbé Morio's scheme for perpetual peace and that it was very interesting but hardly feasible [[cite:C1:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not use the phrase 'ending war forever', but the scheme was the Abbé Morio's plan for perpetual peace.
wrong: Pierre's own scheme, which the Abbé Morio dismissed as hardly feasible.
The sources do not say whose scheme it was, though the Abbé Morio is mentioned.
Prince Andrew's scheme, which Pierre criticised at supper.

correct: Mademoiselle George.
In the vicomte's anecdote the Duc d'Enghien went secretly to Paris to visit Mademoiselle George, the famous actress, and at her house came upon Bonaparte [[cite:C0:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not give her full name, but the actress was Mademoiselle George.
wrong: Mademoiselle George told the anecdote herself at Anna Pávlovna's.
The sources do not name the actress, though George is mentioned in the vicomte's tale.
Mademoiselle Mars, the actress of the Comédie-Française.

correct: Because it was not a war for freedom: helping England and Austria against the greatest man in the world was not right.

Pierre told Prince Andrew that if it were a war for freedom he would be the first to enlist, but to help England and Austria against the greatest man in the world was not right [[cite:C0|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not give a long reason, but Pierre said helping England and Austria against Napoleon was not right.
wrong: Pierre said he would not join because England and Austria were too weak to win, and he did not want to die for a lost cause.
The sources do not state his reason, though England and Austria are mentioned.
Because his father, Count Bezúkhov, forbade him to fight on the side of England and Austria.

correct: Prince Vasíli Kurágin.

Prince Vasíli, Anatole's father, asked Anna Pávlovna to arrange the match and promised to be her 'most devoted slave-slafe with an f' [[cite:C8:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; she answered that she would act on his family's behalf [[cite:C8:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not tag the speaker in that line, but it is Prince Vasíli, who wanted her to arrange a marriage for his son Anatole.
wrong: Anatole, Prince Vasíli's son, promised to be her slafe if she found him a rich wife.
The sources do not say who made the promise, though Prince Vasíli and Anatole are both discussed.
Prince Hippolyte, who wanted Anna Pávlovna to find him a wife.

correct: A place in the Archives Department.
The count complains that Nicholas is leaving the university to enter the army, though there was a place waiting for him in the Archives Department [[cite:C4:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not describe the post in detail, but a place was waiting for him in the Archives Department.
wrong: Borís had a place waiting in the Archives Department before he became an officer.
The sources do not specify the position, beyond a passing mention of the Archives.
A post as first secretary at Vienna.

correct: A second Salomoni.
The count says of Natásha that she will be a singer, "a second Salomoni!", and that they have engaged an Italian to teach her [[cite:C1:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not say who Salomoni was, but the count calls her a second Salomoni.
wrong: The countess says Véra will be a second Salomoni.
The context does not say, though Salomoni is mentioned.
A second Catalani.

correct: She needed five hundred rubles and had only a twenty-five-ruble note.
Anna Mikháylovna told the countess she needed five hundred rubles to equip Borís but had only one twenty-five-ruble note [[cite:C2:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not itemise the uniform, but she said she needed 500 rubles and had only one 25-ruble note.
wrong: She needed twenty-five rubles and had five hundred, all tied up in her lawsuit.
The sources do not give the sums, though five hundred and twenty-five rubles are mentioned.
She needed forty thousand rubles and had nothing at all.

correct: Her son Borís was transferred into the Semënov Guards.

The elderly lady was Princess Drubetskáya (Anna Mikháylovna); Prince Vasíli promised her son would be transferred to the Guards [[cite:C7:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]], and Borís went into the Semënov Guards as a cornet [[cite:C8:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The passages themselves only say 'the Guards', but the knowledge graph places Borís in the Semënov Guards, which he entered as a cornet.
wrong: Prince Vasíli's own son Borís was transferred into the Semënov Guards at his mother's request.
The sources do not say which regiment; the Semënov Guards are mentioned only in the knowledge graph.
Borís was taken onto Kutúzov's staff as his adjutant.

correct: Count Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov.
Borís's godfather is Count Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov; Anna Mikháylovna calls him "Bóry's godfather" [[cite:C2:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not use the word godfather in the petition scene, but Borís's godfather is Count Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov.
wrong: Prince Vasíli is Borís's godfather; Bezúkhov is only his mother's cousin.
The sources do not name the godfather, though Count Bezúkhov is mentioned.
Pierre Bezúkhov is Borís's godfather.

correct: Prince Vasíli hushed it up, but Anatole was still ordered out of Petersburg.
Anatole Kurágin's father, Prince Vasíli, got his son's affair hushed up, but even Anatole was ordered out of Petersburg [[cite:C0:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not name the father in that sentence, but Anatole Kurágin's father (Prince Vasíli) hushed up his son's part, and Anatole was ordered out of Petersburg all the same.
wrong: Prince Vasíli hushed it up, but Anatole was sent back to Moscow like Pierre.
The sources do not say what happened to the son, though Prince Vasíli is said to have hushed things up and someone was ordered out of Petersburg.
Count Bezúkhov hushed up Pierre's part, but Pierre was expelled by the police and sent back to Moscow.

correct: Her brother is Prince Andrew Bolkónski, who is to be Kutúzov's aide-de-camp.

Anna Pávlovna proposed Princess Mary Bolkónskaya for Anatole [[cite:C3:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; her brother, who married Lise Meinen, is an aide-de-camp of Kutúzov's [[cite:C2:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]], and the graph names him Prince Andrew.
The passage about the match does not name the brother, but he is young Bolkónski, Prince Andrew, General Kutúzov's aide-de-camp.
wrong: The bride is Lise Meinen, and her brother Prince Andrew is going to be Kutúzov's aide-de-camp.
The sources do not name the brother, though Prince Andrew and Kutúzov are both mentioned.
Her brother is Prince Andrew, who is to become aide-de-camp to the Emperor.

correct: He went to Anatole Kurágin's gathering, and was afterwards sent back to Moscow.
He broke his word and went to Anatole Kurágin's; after the affair with the bear he was sent back to Moscow.
The text does not say it in one place, but he went to Anatole's and was later sent back to Moscow.
wrong: He went to Dólokhov's and was then sent to Petersburg.
The sources do not say, though Anatole and Moscow are mentioned.
He went to Anatole's and was exiled to the army in the Caucasus.

correct: Márya Ivánovna Dólokhova.

Dólokhov, the officer of the Semënov regiment who drank the rum on the ledge, is the son of Márya Ivánovna Dólokhova, whom a visitor at the Rostóvs' calls 'such a worthy woman' (no context was retrieved, so no chunk can be cited).
The text does not name her in the window scene, but Dólokhov's mother is Márya Ivánovna Dólokhova.
wrong: Márya Ivánovna is Dólokhov's sister.
The sources do not name his mother, though Márya Ivánovna is mentioned.
Márya Lvóvna Karágina.

correct: Prince Vasíli is said to be a rival heir to Count Bezúkhov's fortune.

The man was Prince Vasíli, who brought Pierre and said 'Educate this bear for me!' [[cite:C2:S4|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; in Moscow he is spoken of as Pierre's rival for the fortune of Count Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov.
The retrieved text does not spell out the inheritance, but the man is Prince Vasíli and the fortune is that of the dying Bezúkhov, Pierre's father.
wrong: Pierre, Count Bezúkhov's son, is the rival heir to Prince Vasíli's fortune.
The sources do not say; Prince Vasíli is only linked to Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov through an interaction.
Prince Vasíli is a rival heir to the fortune of Prince Bolkónski, Princess Mary's rich and stingy father.

correct: At Prince Vasíli Kurágin's; they meant to marry Anatole to Prince Andrew's sister.

Pierre was staying at Prince Vasíli Kurágin's and sharing the dissipated life of his son Anatole, whom the family planned to reform by marrying him to Prince Andrew's sister, Princess Mary Bolkónskaya [[cite:C0|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not name her in that sentence, but Pierre stayed at Prince Vasíli Kurágin's, and Anatole was to marry Prince Andrew's sister Mary.
wrong: Pierre was staying at Prince Andrew's, and the Kurágins planned to marry Anatole to Andrew's sister Mary.
The sources do not say where he stayed, though the Kurágin family and Princess Mary are mentioned.
At Prince Vasíli Kurágin's; they planned to marry Anatole to Hélène's friend, the little princess.

correct: She agreed to help with the match between Anatole and her sister-in-law; her sister-in-law's father still had to agree.

In the hall the little princess told Anna Pávlovna 'It is settled' about the match between Anatole and her sister-in-law [[cite:C2:S3|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; Anna Pávlovna asked her to write and say how her father looks at the matter [[cite:C2:S6|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not spell out a promise, but 'It is settled' meant she would back the match of Anatole with her sister-in-law, whose father's view was still needed.
wrong: She promised to marry Anatole herself, if her father agreed.
The sources do not say what was settled, though Anatole and a father are mentioned.
She promised to help with the match for Anatole, but Anatole's father, Prince Vasíli, still had to consent.

correct: Her mother is Márya Lvóvna Karágina.

Julie Karágina turned to young Rostóv at the name day [[cite:C1:S3|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; the knowledge graph records her mother, Márya Lvóvna Karágina, arriving at the Rostóv house with her daughter.
The passages do not state the relationship outright, but the visitor who came with her daughter, Márya Lvóvna Karágina, is Julie's mother.
wrong: Márya Lvóvna Karágina is Julie's aunt; her mother is not named.
The sources do not name her mother, though a Márya Lvóvna Karágina visits the countess.
Her mother is the Countess Rostóva.

correct: For his friend Borís, who was transferred to the Semënov Guards as a cornet.

The count says Nicholas is leaving the university for friendship's sake because his friend Borís has become an officer [[cite:C0:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; Borís got the rank of cornet in the Semënov Guards.
The text here does not give the rank, only that Borís became an officer; the rank was cornet.
wrong: For his friend Borís, who received the rank of colonel in the Guards.
The context does not state the rank, though Borís is mentioned as a cornet.
For Prince Andrew, who became a cornet in the Horse Guards.

correct: Prince Vasíli got him into the Guards; she hopes Count Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov, his godfather, will pay for the equipment.

She applied to Prince Vasíli, who put the matter before the Emperor [[cite:C4:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]], and now pins her hope on Count Cyril Vladímirovich Bezúkhov, Borís's godfather, to equip him [[cite:C2:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not call either man a grandee, but the transfer came through Prince Vasíli and she hopes Count Bezúkhov, Bóry's godfather, will provide for his equipment.
wrong: Prince Vasíli got the transfer, and she hopes the count - her host, Count Rostóv - will pay for the equipment.
The sources do not name the second patron, though Prince Vasíli and Count Bezúkhov are both mentioned.
Prince Golítsyn arranged the transfer through Rumyántsev; she hopes Prince Vasíli, Borís's father, will pay for the equipment.

correct: At the Rostóvs'; the countess and her youngest daughter are both named Nataly.

Borís was brought up at his mother's rich relations, the Rostóvs [[cite:C4:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]], and the name day is St. Natalia's day for the mother and youngest daughter, both named Nataly [[cite:C4:S4|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not say who paid for his schooling, but he was educated from childhood at the Rostóvs', where mother and daughter share the name Nataly.
wrong: Borís was educated at Prince Vasíli's in Petersburg; the two Rostóv ladies are both named Nataly.
The sources do not say where he was educated, though the Rostóvs celebrate St. Natalia's day.
At the Rostóvs'; the countess and her daughter are both called Natásha.

correct: In Russian; he had promised to take the vicomte home.

Hippolyte told his Moscow story in Russian, "or the point will be lost" [[cite:C0|war_and_peace_book1.txt]], and afterwards waited in the porch for the vicomte, Mortemart, whom he had promised to take home [[cite:C4:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not say why Russian was needed, but he told it in Russian and promised to take the vicomte home.
wrong: In French, apologising to the vicomte that it was not in Russian; he promised to take Pierre home.
The sources do not say whom he promised to take home, though he told the story in Russian to the vicomte.
In Russian; he had promised to take the little princess home.

correct: She calls him 'Uncle' and will live in the country with Andrew's father and sister.

Lise calls her husband 'Uncle's aide-de-camp', Kutúzov having taken Andrew as aide-de-camp; Andrew reminds her she will be in the country 'with my father and sister' (no context was retrieved, so no chunk can be cited).
The text does not say outright that 'Uncle' means Kutúzov, but she calls him Uncle, and she will stay with Andrew's father and sister.
wrong: She calls Kutúzov 'the old fox' and will live with her own father and sister.
The sources do not say, though an uncle, a father and a sister are mentioned.
She calls him 'Uncle' and will live with Anna Pávlovna in Petersburg.

correct: With Prince Vasíli, at the Rumyántsovs' theatricals.
The countess says she has not seen Prince Vasíli since they acted together at the Rumyántsovs' theatricals, and that he paid her attentions in those days.
The text does not describe the play, but she acted with Prince Vasíli at the Rumyántsovs'.
wrong: With Count Rostóv, her husband, at the Rumyántsovs' theatricals.
The sources do not say, though Prince Vasíli and the Rumyántsovs are mentioned.
With Prince Vasíli, at Rumyántsev's, the minister Anna Mikháylovna was told to appeal to.

correct: The count is Ilyá; Dmítri Vasílevich manages all his affairs.
The countess addresses her husband as Ilyá, and his affairs are run by Dmítri Vasílevich, a man of good family and the manager of all his affairs [[cite:C3:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not give his full name, but the countess calls him Ilyá, and Dmítri Vasílevich manages his affairs.
wrong: The count is Dmítri, and his affairs are managed by Ilyá.
The context does not name the count, though Ilyá and Dmítri are mentioned.
The count is Nicholas, and Dmítri Vasílevich is his steward.

correct: Sónya, the count's niece; Nicholas copied out verses for her.

The girl is Sónya, the count's fifteen-year-old niece [[cite:C6:S2|war_and_peace_book1.txt]]; Nicholas later copied out some verses for her, the first he had ever written (no retrieved chunk holds this second fact).
The text does not show the copying scene directly, but the girl is Sónya, and Nicholas copied out some verses for her.
wrong: Natásha's sister Véra; Nicholas copied out verses for her.
The sources do not say who she is, though Sónya and some verses are mentioned.
Sónya; Nicholas copied out a letter to Borís for her.

correct: On the march to Radzivílov.
Borís had stayed in Moscow for his equipment and was to join the Guards on their march to Radzivílov [[cite:C1:S3|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
The text does not say where exactly he would catch up, only that he was to join them on the march to Radzivílov.
wrong: He was to join them in Petersburg, before they marched from Radzivílov.
The sources do not specify the place, though Radzivílov is named as the Guards' destination.
He was to join them at Olmütz.

correct: He asks her, if the old count is better, to invite Pierre to dine with them.
The count asks Anna Mikháylovna, if Count Cyril Vladímirovich is better, to ask Pierre to dine with the Rostóvs, since he has been to the house and danced with the children.
The text does not dwell on the disgrace, but the count asks her to invite Pierre to dine.
wrong: He asks her to tell Pierre not to dine with them, because of the disgrace.
The sources do not say, though Pierre may dine with the Rostóvs.
He asks her to bring Pierre to the ball that evening.

correct: Anna Pávlovna Schérer.
The hostess was Anna Pávlovna Schérer, maid of honor and favorite of the Empress Márya Fëdorovna [[cite:C0:S1|war_and_peace_book1.txt]].
